title: Reserve Bank holds interest rates at 4.10%, what it means for your mortgage and savings
excerpt: The Reserve Bank kept the official interest rate on hold at 4.10 per cent at its August meeting. We break down what that means for borrowers, savers, and first-home buyers.
body:
The Reserve Bank of Australia, the country's central bank, kept the official interest rate on hold at 4.10 per cent at its August meeting. That is the third hold in a row. Most economists had expected no change, after July's inflation number came in at 2.7 per cent, which is comfortably inside the Reserve Bank's 2 to 3 per cent target.

In the statement that came with the decision, Governor Michele Bullock said the Board is still 'data-dependent', meaning they want to see more evidence that inflation is sustainably back at the target before cutting rates. Pay growth is still running at about 3.7 per cent, which is above the level the Reserve Bank considers consistent with stable prices.

The market is now pricing a 60 per cent chance of a rate cut before Christmas, with the first cut fully priced in for early 2027.

Our take: the Reserve Bank is being more cautious than the market expected. They are worried that inflation, the rate at which prices in general are going up, might stick around if wages keep growing faster than productivity. Until we see a few more months of inflation around 2.5 per cent or lower, the Reserve Bank is unlikely to cut. That means variable mortgage rates stay high for the rest of this year, and term deposit rates stay around 4.5 to 5 per cent.
whatItMeans: If you have a variable-rate home loan, where the interest rate moves up and down with the Reserve Bank: Your monthly repayment does not change this month. If you have a $600,000 loan at an average 6.0 per cent variable rate, you are paying about $3,600 a month, the same as last month.

If your fixed-rate home loan, where the interest rate is locked in for a set period, is ending in the next three to six months: Lenders are quietly trimming their two- and three-year fixed offers. It is worth shopping around before any rate cut gets priced in.

If you have money in a term deposit, where you lock in a set interest rate for a set period, or a bonus saver account: Rates are unlikely to improve until the Reserve Bank actually cuts. The big four banks are still offering 4.5 to 5.0 per cent on 12-month term deposits.

If you are trying to buy your first home: The rules around how much you can borrow are still tight. Banks test whether you could afford the repayments at your interest rate plus 3 per cent, so today's rates are still limiting how much you can borrow.
